Iran In Perspective: maybe Iran's political situation today was shaped by the US/UK overthrow of Iran's democratically elected prime minister in 1953

From Wikipedia:

"In August 2013, 60 years after, the American Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) admitted that it was involved in both the planning and the execution of the coup, including the bribing of Iranian politicians, security and army high-ranking officials, as well as pro-coup propaganda.[11][12] The CIA is quoted acknowledging the coup was carried out "under CIA direction" and "as an act of U.S. foreign policy, conceived and approved at the highest levels of government."

I think that it's hard to understand the current US/Iran situation without understanding that generations of Iranian leaders viewed the world in the context of their country's leader having been overthrown in a US/UK backed coup, their nation destabilized and then devolved from a moderate, prosperous country into dictatorship then into a crappy theocracy.

They didn't do it because they were bored. They did it to protect hundreds of millions if not billions of money in investments made in Iran, and to protect the time left on the legal agreements they had signed with Iran that Iran said would not be broken. The new government was going to take the money and void the legal agreements.

Also most people and especially minorities had tons more civil rights under the Shah than under the Ayatollah.

Even if it was hundreds of billions, I'm not sure that morally excuses overthrowing a democratic government... post-WWII, the US and other countries have generally lived by a commercial framework of international courts and it's clear that countries (including the US) renege on commercial agreements regularly. Also, it's their oil - if they wanted to take it back, it's kind of their right (and it's also totally fair for the US/UK to stop trading with them as a consequence). But to destroy a democracy - I don't think that's morally acceptable and certainly now we can see that the after effects were disastrous for both the country and the region.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_the_Imperial_State_of_Iran

I think that the Ayatollah was largely in reaction to the Shah, but yes, the Ayatollah is not a nice person - again, I'm not saying that either side is right or wrong (because that is pretty dependent on what your values or interests are, which side of the story you sit on), but it's clear that these actions shaped what is happening today.
The same is partially (but to a much lesser degree) true in regards to North Korea. The U.S. destroyed virtually all buildings and civilized locations in North Korea.

To play devil's advocate:

Western companies had invested millions in Iran. There were legally binding contracts signed with the old Iranian government.

The Prime Minister they elected was going to void these legal contracts and essentially seize all of the money and property poured in the country by the West.

The West said, "fuck you, you will honor your word to us, and you will not steal our money." Then we got the Shah. Under the Shah, Christians and Jews were not persecuted, nor were women beaten if they went out and forgot their hijab. In fact you might even see a woman in a bikini on the beach. The country was socially liberal and protected minorities.

Now if you miss Friday prayers and get stoned to death in the town square. No Jews, No Christians, or if there are any left they are under oppression and prejudiced taxation for not converting.

I agree that there are two sides of every story, and I'm not disagreeing with everything you wrote (as devil's advocate). There are two things that I think are still wrong with the situation... one is that we overthrew their democratically elected leader over what was essentially a commercial dispute. That's not right. There are international courts and such, and countries (including the US) renege on contracts and business agreements all the time, it's not fair to execute a coup, especially if we value or at least want to pretend that we value democracy.

Second was that Iran was pretty moderate under Mossadegh and he implemented many major reforms for the benefit of the common person, according to Wikipedia, "unemployment compensation was introduced, factory owners were ordered to pay benefits to sick and injured workers, and peasants were freed from forced labor in their landlords' estates. Twenty percent of the money landlords received in rent was placed in a fund to pay for development projects such as public baths, rural housing, and pest control". Life under the Shah before Mossadegh was pretty totalitarian and definitely a type of kleptocracy with little regard for human rights. The return of the Shah saw major human rights abuses including kidnappings and torture of political enemies that numbered in the thousands.

So, we can either support democracy, the will of the people, and the right to self-determination, or we can just accept that sometimes we have to do pretty shitty things to preserve our strategic/economic goals at the expense of other nations and their people.
